core: score, song selection, cue, and leitmotif

claims.claim: Cinematic sound design includes music alongside dialogue, sound effects, ambience, and silence, and sound can operate co-expressively with moving image.
Diegetic music is presented as part of the world of the film and available to characters, while nondiegetic music is presented outside that immediate world for the audience.
Silent-film screenings commonly used musical accompaniment before synchronized sound became standard in cinema.

A film score is music composed for a particular motion picture, while preexisting songs can be selected for a film and may be diegetic or nondiegetic; soundtrack has both a broad audio-track meaning and a common album meaning.
A sound bridge overlaps sound across a cut, including audio that begins before a shot or continues from a previous shot, and can connect scenes or shots.
A leitmotif is a recurring musical association with a character or other narrative element, and changes in its context can support analysis of a film's themes or story development.
Music may support, shape, or contrast with a moving image, so an interpretation should cite cue timing, audible features, repetition, and visual context rather than assume one universal emotion.
